Q1

A defensible leading mechanism is that X and Y jointly reorganize the crystallization pathway into a more coherent, less strained final lattice. X supplies chloride-bearing chemistry that participates in the common transient hexagonal-polytype sequence, while Y provides a preformed layered-perovskite template that biases nucleation and orientation. If the final film inherits better crystallographic alignment and lower residual microstrain, it should contain fewer grain-boundary and strain-related defect populations. Those defects can act as nonradiative recombination centers and chemically active sites, so their reduction would plausibly slow photo-thermal degradation and delay decomposition during the harsh light-and-temperature ramp. This mechanism directly links observation 1 (shared transient sequence) and observation 2 (improved orientation/lower microstrain) to observation 3 (later decomposition). The strongest competing explanation is that X+Y simply changes surface morphology, thickness, roughness, or local optical absorption, thereby altering heat distribution or apparent stability without changing the intrinsic lattice pathway. That hypothesis is credible because the reported morphology was not independently matched across treatments. The evidence boundary is therefore large: transient-phase similarity and final structural metrics do not prove that every intermediate is beneficial, nor do they rule out uncontrolled morphology, composition, or interface effects. A causal test would hold film thickness, roughness, and morphology constant while varying X, Y, and X+Y; track the full time-resolved phase sequence; quantify residual strain and defect density; and correlate those variables with degradation kinetics.

Q2

The decisive comparison is not the absolute lifetime of the two films but whether their chemical and structural states follow the same sequence under identical stress. The experiment should begin by matching initial absorber composition, thickness, grain size, orientation, defect density, and device stack as closely as possible; otherwise a lower initial defect population can masquerade as a different pathway. During controlled illumination, heat, humidity, or combined MPP aging, the two films should be sampled at matched elapsed time and matched accumulated dose. In situ or frequent ex situ GIWAXS/XRD should track the appearance and growth rate of the 2D phase, while depth-resolved ToF-SIMS or XPS maps Cl, PbI2, iodine species, and organic-cation redistribution. PL/TRPL, electroluminescence, SCLC, and impedance should monitor recombination and transport, and post-stress microscopy should quantify morphology. A different trajectory is supported if the seed-containing film develops a qualitatively distinct intermediate, changes the order of phase formation, localizes degradation differently, or shows a new kinetic regime even when the final endpoint resembles the control. A slower same-trajectory mechanism is supported if both films pass through the same phases in the same order and the seed film merely has a longer induction period or reduced rate constant. The remaining ambiguity is that matched initial morphology does not guarantee identical local chemistry, and frequent sampling can perturb the system. Therefore, the conclusion should be conditional on the matched controls and repeated across several stress conditions.

Q3

The strongest update is that X+Y changes the kinetic pathway of degradation. The Y-only sequence—yellow 2H-FAPI followed by 2H-PbI2—is consistent with a conventional decomposition route in which the black FA-based perovskite first converts to a metastable 2H polymorph before forming the more familiar 2H PbI2 termination. The X+Y film avoids detectable 2H-FAPI and delays formation of 3R-PbI2, so the combined treatment can be interpreted as raising the activation barrier or blocking the intermediate that normally accelerates conversion. This is stronger than saying the final product is simply “better,” because the same final 3R-PbI2-like product can appear at very different times. The X-only result is especially important: if X alone produced the same unusual product rapidly, X would not be protective by itself; instead, its beneficial effect requires the specific interaction with Y. Thus the mechanism should be framed around trajectory control and delayed onset, not merely product identity. The unresolved causal variable is whether the delay arises from altered defect chemistry, modified surface/interfacial energetics, changed ion-migration pathways, residual strain, or a combination of these. A decisive follow-up would compare X, Y, and X+Y with matched initial defect densities and track the time-resolved appearance of 2H-FAPI, 3R-PbI2, and any intermediate signatures while independently measuring ion migration and interfacial recombination.

Q4

The decisive distinction is whether the additive/seed combination changes the sequence of failure modes, not just how fast they occur. If X+Y changes the accessible trajectory, MPP-aged devices should show a different order or set of dominant signatures from the control. For example, the control might first develop local halide segregation, then interfacial recombination and finally a structural transition toward non-perovskite phases, whereas the treated device suppresses or delays the early trigger and instead shows a later, mechanistically distinct failure such as ion redistribution at a different interface, electrode reaction, or a different crystallization pathway. The treated population should also have a different distribution of failure times and failure modes, not simply a longer mean time to the same endpoint.

If X+Y merely slows the same route, the normalized degradation curves should be approximately parallel on a suitable kinetic scale, and the spectroscopic, spatial and structural signatures should appear in the same order. A simple increase in T80 without a change in mechanism would support this weaker claim.

Useful predictions include: (1) under continuous MPP stress, the treated film should retain its initial bandgap and phase identity longer while the control develops the known early warning signal; (2) post-aging depth profiles should show less accumulation of mobile species at the vulnerable interface; (3) the seed should remain detectable or leave a characteristic structural signature associated with delayed conversion; (4) the effect should persist across several devices and be sensitive to removing either X or Y if both are mechanistically required.

Alternative explanations must be considered. Improved initial coverage, lower trap density, better contact selectivity or altered optical absorption could extend lifetime without changing the degradation pathway. Chloride may volatilize or redistribute, creating a transient benefit followed by a new failure mode. The layered seed could act as a physical barrier rather than a chemical stabilizer. Conversely, the treatment could suppress one degradation channel but accelerate another, such as electrode corrosion or moisture ingress through altered morphology.

The interpretation would be weakened if the treated and control devices fail through identical intermediate states, if the benefit disappears after short preconditioning, if the seed is consumed before aging begins, or if the improvement is confined to one stress condition and reverses under another. A strong falsification would be a statistically significant change in the dominant failure mode for the control but not for the treated device, together with direct evidence that X+Y alters the relevant chemical or structural transition.

Q1

The most direct diagnosis is a spacer-controlled adsorption-topology mechanism. All four molecules contain the same anchoring motif and terminal CF3 group, so the dominant variable is how the spacer changes conformational freedom, dipole distribution, and lateral packing on the perovskite surface. A larger nano-IR active fraction together with smaller aggregates indicates that L3 distributes more uniformly and avoids dense, poorly contacted islands. Uniform molecular coverage can passivate undercoordinated Pb-related defects and reduce trap-assisted recombination, explaining the higher acceptor-free PL lifetime and QFLS. At the same time, a thin, continuous, electronically favorable interface can improve contact with C60 and reduce extraction barriers, consistent with the reversed lifetime trend after C60 deposition and lower series resistance. The absence of a new low-dimensional phase argues against a simple 2D-capping explanation; the effect is therefore best described as molecularly mediated surface reconstruction and contact engineering rather than formation of a thick insulating overlayer.

The strongest alternative is that the ranking is dominated by retention or electrostatics rather than adsorption topology. In that case, L3 may simply remain on the surface longer during annealing, solvent exposure, or C60 deposition, or its dipole may create a more favorable energy offset. The same lifetime and resistance trends could then arise from better chemical/electrostatic coverage even if the spatial distribution were similar.

A decisive test would compare adsorption topology and retention independently. Measure the initial surface fraction and aggregate size immediately after treatment, then repeat after identical thermal and processing steps. If L3 starts with superior uniformity and retains it, the topology hypothesis is strengthened. If all ligands begin similarly but L3 alone preserves coverage, retention becomes the leading explanation. Independent electrostatic measurements—such as Kelvin-probe work-function mapping, surface-potential calculations, and energy-level alignment before and after C60—would test whether the ranking follows dipole magnitude. Finally, a thickness series should show that the beneficial effect saturates at a monolayer-like regime and degrades when the layer becomes too thick; otherwise a blocking-layer explanation cannot be excluded. Because buried-interface orientation is not measured, the conclusion remains limited to the accessible top-surface and electrical signatures.

Q2

A topology-specific conclusion requires holding the chemical anchor and terminal group constant while varying only the spacer geometry. The reported L0-L3 series is useful because all contain the same amidinium-type anchoring motif and CF3 terminus, so differences can be attributed more plausibly to spacer topology than to a completely different functional group. However, the four molecules can still differ in adsorption strength, surface coverage, orientation, dipole moment, Lewis-base character, steric packing, and electronic coupling to C60. Those variables must be measured separately.

First, quantify what actually remains on the film. XPS or ToF-SIMS should determine the absolute amount of each ligand after annealing and washing, while contact-angle, ellipsometry, AFM, and GIWAXS/GIXRD should test whether the spacer changes surface roughness, wetting, or molecular ordering. A topology effect is weakened if one molecule simply leaves a much thicker or more discontinuous layer.

Second, probe binding and electronic structure on the bare perovskite. FTIR shifts of the amidinium-related vibrations, NMR or DFT binding calculations, and XPS shifts of Pb/I species can reveal whether the spacer alters coordination geometry or electron donation. UPS/KPFM should measure work-function and band-edge shifts; a consistent trend across L0-L3 would support a dipole/orientation contribution, whereas scattered shifts would suggest uncontrolled coverage or packing effects. TRPL on bare films can show whether the ligand passivates surface traps, but it cannot prove improved extraction through C60.

Third, test the complete interface. SCLC or dark J-V should measure trap density and leakage, while transient photovoltage/photocurrent, impedance, and PL quenching after C60 deposition should distinguish slower recombination from faster electron transfer. A beneficial topology should improve both bare-film lifetime/passivation and contacted extraction without increasing series resistance.

A decisive control would be a pair of molecules with nearly identical dipole and Lewis basicity but different spacer rigidity or packing, plus a deliberately mismatched coverage control. If the best device follows spacer topology after coverage and dipole are normalized, the topology argument is strong. If performance follows retained amount or work-function shift instead, the original series is confounded.

Q3

The two conclusions are each incomplete. A shorter contacted TRPL decay can mean faster transfer into C60, but it can also mean a more lossy interface if the ligand creates traps, leaves a conductive residue, or changes morphology. The acceptor-free lifetime and QFLS provide the necessary counterbalance: if the ligand improves intrinsic recombination while simultaneously accelerating the contacted decay, productive extraction becomes more plausible. The series trend—acceptor-free lifetime rising from roughly 280 to 750 ns, QFLS increasing from about 1.24 to 1.29 eV, and the C60 conduction-band offset decreasing from 0.13 to 0.03 eV—is consistent with better passivation plus improved energetic alignment. However, the energy-level shift alone cannot prove that the ligand forms a spatially favorable electronic bridge. It could instead reflect a surface dipole, a change in work function, or altered band bending without improving molecular coupling.

The decisive test must separate three variables: intrinsic defect density, interfacial electronic coupling, and energetic alignment. First, measure acceptor-free PL/TRPL and QFLS on the same ligand series to confirm that the fastest contacted decay does not come at the cost of higher bulk/surface recombination. Second, quantify the actual ligand coverage and orientation using XPS, NMR, FTIR, or ToF-SIMS together with GIWAXS/GIXRD and AFM/KPFM. If the best ligand has a moderate, uniform coverage and a spacer geometry that places the terminal group near the C60 contact, that supports the topology hypothesis. Third, use transient absorption or ultrafast pump-probe with C60 present to extract an independent electron-transfer rate, and compare it with the TRPL-derived rate. Fourth, vary the C60 thickness or add an ultrathin interlayer to test whether the effect scales with electronic coupling rather than merely with a static energy offset. Finally, fabricate devices with matched Voc and fill factor but different ligand topologies; if the series retains high voltage while Jsc and FF improve, the mechanism is more likely extraction-enhancing. A purely dipole explanation would predict similar behavior for any ligand producing the same work-function shift, whereas the observed spacer-dependent trend argues against that. The strongest conclusion is therefore conditional: the combined lifetime/QFLS/offset/device evidence favors productive extraction through a topology-controlled interface, but it does not exclude a contribution from dipole alignment unless those controls are performed.

Q4

The observations establish that the spacer series can tune surface chemistry and that one member, L3, produces a substantial voltage-driven efficiency gain in the reported small-area inverted device. The proposed mechanism is plausible because the spacer changes adsorption geometry, which can alter both defect passivation and electronic coupling to C60. However, the module result is not a direct proof of transferability: it uses a different front-contact process and an iodide-rich composition, so the same ligand function cannot be assumed without matched controls and identical architecture. The outdoor result is also incomplete. A 14.2% loss over 258 days is meaningful, but comparing it with a 27-day control does not establish relative durability. The test lacks matched encapsulation, area, spectral exposure, temperature, humidity, MPP operation, and failure-mode analysis. It also does not determine whether the ligand remains chemically intact or merely delays an unrelated degradation pathway. Confidence would increase if the same L0-L3 series were tested in the module architecture with matched controls, if adsorption topology was measured directly on the relevant surface, and if post-aging spectroscopy showed ligand retention or decomposition. Spatial PL/QFLS, contact-resistance measurements, and controlled thermal/humidity/light protocols would connect the molecular design to the observed voltage gain and durability.

Q1

The additional benefit of K+UV should be attributed to UV-assisted formation of a more robust modifier-derived low-dimensional network. The thioether-containing ammonium-chloride molecule can coordinate Pb sites and organize into a low-dimensional phase, but its terminal alkene provides a handle for covalent crosslinking. Deep-UV exposure during annealing can initiate radical reactions among those alkenes, converting a loosely assembled modifier layer into a more interconnected, mechanically coherent barrier. This mechanism explains why K+UV shows a more ordered modifier-derived low-dimensional phase than K alone: the same molecular species is present in both cases, but UV provides the chemical pathway to link them. It also explains the reduced bias-induced microstrain and iodide redistribution, because a crosslinked low-dimensional network can better constrain grain-boundary motion, suppress ion migration pathways, and resist mechanical deformation under electrical stress. The causal chain is therefore modifier coordination plus UV-initiated crosslinking → denser/ordered low-dimensional phase → lower strain and ion redistribution → improved operational stability.

The strongest competing explanation is that deep-UV exposure simply changes the annealing history through photo-thermal heating, altered crystallization kinetics, or non-specific photochemical damage/healing. The UV lamp could raise local temperature, change solvent evaporation, modify defect populations, or promote a different modifier orientation without any alkene crosslinking. That would also improve PL lifetime and reduce ion migration if it produced a more favorable morphology.

The evidence boundary is that the reported experiment does not isolate UV chemistry from heat. Because deep-UV exposure occurs during thermal annealing, the K+UV condition cannot be compared with K as a clean test of crosslinking unless matched controls are used. A decisive design would include a thermally matched no-UV control, a UV-only no-anneal control, and a chemically matched modifier lacking the terminal alkene but otherwise similar. Crosslinking would be supported by direct chemical signatures such as loss of C=C character, new crosslink-related vibrational modes, increased resistance to solvent extraction, or network-mechanical measurements, together with the observed ordering and ion-migration suppression. Without those controls, the correct conclusion is limited to an association between deep-UV processing and improved structural/ion-migration behavior, not proof that alkene crosslinking is the unique cause.

Q2

The decisive experiment must vary the reactive functionality while holding the rest of the molecule and the process as constant as possible. The best control set would include M, a thioether analogue without the terminal alkene, and an alkene analogue without the thioether. All three should receive identical K treatment and then either no UV or the same deep-UV dose. If stabilization requires the alkene, only the alkene-containing molecules should gain the additional benefit under UV; if it is a generic UV/thermal effect, all modifiers should improve similarly after irradiation; if it is ordinary passivation, the UV step should add little beyond the chemical treatment. Direct reaction evidence should then be obtained on the film surface or at the relevant interface. XPS or NMR can track changes in sulfur and carbon environments, while FTIR/Raman can monitor disappearance or shift of the alkene signature and formation of new bonds. Depth profiling or isotope labeling would help determine whether the reaction occurs at the intended location rather than throughout the bulk. An orthogonal functional test should connect the chemical change to a mechanism-sensitive property, such as trap density, ion-migration barrier, interfacial recombination, or stress relaxation, rather than relying only on PCE. The remaining boundary is that a successful alkene-specific correlation does not prove a single covalent bond; it could involve radical-mediated cross-linking, altered crystallization, or coupled passivation. Conversely, a negative result does not exclude a useful but non-covalent UV-assisted process. The conclusion should therefore be limited to the demonstrated chemical and functional correlation unless independent structure determination and long-term operational controls are added.

Q3

The crosslink-specific mechanism should be retained but narrowed. The disappearance of the C=C feature near 1633 cm−1 after deep-UV, together with the analogous loss of alkene-associated bands and appearance of C–C-related features in a pure low-dimensional model film, supports the idea that the terminal alkene undergoes a UV-induced reaction. Because no new degradation-related FTIR features are observed under the same short treatment, the result is more consistent with constructive modification of the alkene-containing species than with gross photochemical decomposition. This strengthens the proposed pathway in which deep-UV converts a kinetically incorporated, noncovalent modifier population into a more strongly bound or networked modifier-derived phase. It does not, however, prove that the resulting structure is a continuous covalent polymer, nor does it show where the reacted species reside in the mixed-cation film. The reaction could be localized at grain boundaries, buried interfaces, surface clusters, or within a low-dimensional phase, and the FTIR signal integrates over all accessible chemical environments. A defensible revision is therefore: deep-UV activates the alkene moiety and changes its local bonding environment, plausibly increasing mechanical/ionic stabilization, but the exact topology and spatial distribution of the crosslinked network remain unresolved. Direct evidence would require depth-resolved spectroscopy, chemical mapping, crosslinking-density measurements, and comparison with an alkene-free analogue matched for the thioether and ammonium functions.

Q4

The transferred process should still show a UV-dependent chemical signature, but its magnitude may be reduced by the lower dose and substrate attenuation. A supportive result would be a monotonic increase in the alkene-derived product signal from K to K+UV, accompanied by stronger or more uniform mechanical reinforcement and lower ion-migration indicators. The product signal should correlate with the spatial region receiving sufficient UV, so mapping through the substrate thickness or using a calibrated optical model is essential. Mechanically, the film should become less prone to crack propagation or stress relaxation without becoming brittle; ion-mobility measurements should show slower migration or larger activation barriers. Device stability should improve relative to K, especially under heat and illumination, while initial passivation gains remain present.

Generic passivation would appear if K and K+UV give similar chemical, mechanical and ionic responses despite the UV step. Incomplete activation would show a weak or discontinuous product signal, strong near-surface modification but little change deeper in the film, and only modest stability improvement. Depth-nonuniform reaction would produce a gradient in the alkene-derived signal, local mechanical stiffening, and possibly new interfacial defects where the reaction is too abrupt. A control lacking the terminal alkene is critical because it separates true alkene photochemistry from UV-induced damage or unrelated thermal effects. The prediction should therefore be conditional on dose, wavelength, substrate transmission and reaction kinetics, not simply on whether UV was applied.

Q1

The leading mechanism is a stage-dependent role of M-derived chemistry. During precursor processing and thermal formation, M participates in transient coordination or intermediate-species chemistry that lowers the kinetic barrier for Br/I mixing, producing a more homogeneous wide-bandgap absorber. This explains why M improves halide mixing during formation and why it does not need to undergo a visible dark thermal transformation near the annealing temperature: its useful effect is embedded in the evolving precursor/film chemistry. After the film is formed, the same molecular family can act differently when applied as P on the surface. P may bind undercoordinated sites, passivate defects, alter local strain or ion-migration pathways, and therefore suppress light-induced halide redistribution without needing to recreate the bulk mixing process. Its weaker performance in a separate thermal-mixing model is consistent with this division of labor: P is optimized for stabilization of an existing lattice, not for driving initial compositional homogenization.

The strongest non-identity-change alternative is that M and P differ mainly in physical location, concentration, and defect/strain state. M incorporated into the precursor could improve crystallization, reduce grain-boundary disorder, and create a more uniform initial composition, while surface P could block ion migration or passivate surface traps. Light-induced redistribution would then be suppressed by reduced defect-assisted transport rather than by a new operating-state chemical species. This alternative is plausible because the identity and amount of M-derived species are not directly quantified in operating devices.

The key evidence boundary is that the proposed operating-state chemical transformation remains unproven. Direct operando identification of M-derived species, depth-resolved composition before and after illumination, and matched controls that vary only incorporation route and loading are needed. Without them, the mechanism should be stated as a stage-dependent coordination/passivation hypothesis supported by formation and post-treatment comparisons, not as demonstrated in-device chemistry.

Q2

The decisive experiment is to compare the chemical state of M before and after the same light exposure that produces the performance change, while keeping the mixed-halide composition and device stack fixed. The as-prepared film should be characterized by XPS, FTIR/Raman, solid-state NMR, mass spectrometry or another method sensitive to the proposed M/P chemistry. After controlled illumination at the relevant wavelength, temperature and atmosphere, the same measurements should be repeated on the same composition. A light-induced mechanism requires a new or substantially changed chemical signature only after illumination, with a magnitude correlated to the device response. An inherited mechanism predicts that the beneficial chemical state is already present in the dark-fabricated film and does not require further photochemical conversion.

Phase and ionic controls are needed because the mixed-halide absorber can independently undergo halide segregation. Time-resolved PL, spatial PL mapping, GIWAXS/XRD and depth profiling should track whether bandgap narrowing, Br/I redistribution or crystallinity changes occur. If M suppresses those signatures without forming a new illuminated chemical state, the benefit is more consistent with pre-existing passivation or phase stabilization. If a new M-derived species appears only after light and coincides with reduced segregation or improved transport, the light-induced pathway becomes plausible.

The separate synthesis of P is useful only if P can be identified in the illuminated film and its concentration tracks the performance gain. Controls should include untreated mixed-halide films, M-treated films measured in the dark, P-doped films, and a chemically similar but inactive analogue. Dose, illumination dose, temperature and encapsulation must be held constant. The conclusion should remain conditional unless the same causal pattern is reproduced across multiple devices and the proposed chemical state is directly detected in the operating film.

Q3

The observation supports retaining the broad idea that M participates in a light-driven chemical transformation, but it requires narrowing the claim. The new 19F NMR signal after 24 h of UV-containing ambient illumination matches independently synthesized P, so it is reasonable to propose that M converts at least partially into P under illumination. The roughly 30% estimate and additional weak signals indicate that the conversion is incomplete and that other photochemical products may form. This is consistent with a mechanism in which M is useful during thermal film formation and then generates a different species during operation that could influence halide redistribution. It does not, however, prove that P is the active stabilizing species in the mixed-halide front cell. The experiment uses a high-loading MAPbI3 film, not necessarily the final mixed-halide composition or device stack, and the illumination condition includes UV light and ambient air. Therefore, the causal chain remains incomplete: one must show that P forms under the actual tandem-relevant spectrum and atmosphere, determine its spatial distribution, quantify how much is needed to suppress iodide/bromide segregation, and demonstrate that the same chemistry improves operational stability without creating traps or transport barriers. A defensible updated mechanism is conditional: M is a precursor that can generate P and possibly other species under illumination; P is a plausible candidate for suppressing mixed-halide redistribution, but its identity, concentration, location, and functional role in the operating device require direct validation.

Q4

Transfer is plausible but not established. The favorable pattern would be: (1) the same P-related chemical signature appears in a low-loading, hermetically encapsulated mixed-halide film after realistic tandem-relevant illumination; (2) P forms at a rate compatible with the onset of suppressed halide segregation; (3) the effect persists when oxygen is excluded, showing that ambient air is not required; (4) P is absent or inactive in the no-M control; and (5) the device retains its bandgap and voltage under continuous operation while the control segregates. A falsifying pattern would be rapid disappearance of P in the absence of oxygen, no detectable P at device-relevant loading, or suppression of segregation even when P does not form. The latter outcome would imply that M acts through another route—such as precursor coordination, altered crystallization, lower trap density, changed ion-migration barriers, or a different photoproduct—not through the detected P. Ambient-air detection is therefore mechanistically suggestive, not proof of relevance. The experiment should also test whether P accumulates to a harmful level, blocks transport, or changes optical absorption. A rigorous transfer study needs identical composition and encapsulation, controlled oxygen and humidity levels, matched illumination spectra, time-resolved chemical tracking, and post-illumination depth profiling. If P is only transient or requires oxygen, the design must either preserve the necessary environment or identify an oxygen-independent active species.

Q1

A defensible mechanism is that X acts as a humidity-buffered interfacial template during the early conversion stage. The thin ionic organic layer can adsorb or organize water molecules and alter local ion mobility, lowering the kinetic barrier for the sequential PbI2/organic-salt reaction while keeping the water activity within a useful window. This would explain faster and more uniform conversion under moderate humidity. In dry nitrogen, the same mechanism fails because the required water-mediated pathway is absent; the persistent lead iodide in both films shows that X does not replace the need for moisture. At excessive humidity, the buffer is overwhelmed, leading to overreaction, decomposition, and voids. The reduction in trap-related losses is therefore a consequence of a more complete and uniform conversion plus possible surface passivation, not independent proof that X changed the conversion kinetics. The strongest competing explanation is that X simply changes precursor wetting, thickness, or nucleation density, with humidity acting independently. To distinguish these possibilities, one should measure water uptake and mobility near X, track phase evolution in situ under controlled humidity, compare dry-N2 and humid conditions with matched morphology, and use a chemically similar but non-ionic/non-hygroscopic control. The main boundary is that the supplied observations do not quantify water content, ion flux, or the exact chemical role of X, so the mechanism remains conditional on the humidity window and cannot be generalized from electronic-quality measurements alone.

Q2

The decisive experiment is a time-resolved structural study of the same precursor stack with and without treatment X during the anneal. In situ GIWAXS or XRD should track the disappearance of the precursor phase, the appearance and growth rate of the perovskite Bragg peaks, and any transient intermediate phases. If treatment X changes the conversion pathway, it should shift the onset time, accelerate or suppress specific intermediates, or alter the sequence of crystallization events. A parallel optical absorption or PL measurement can test whether the electronic bandgap and radiative quality evolve together with those structural transitions. Chemical evidence should then show that the ionic organic layer remains associated with the film rather than being removed before conversion; depth profiling, XPS, ToF-SIMS, or isotope-labeled tracking can establish its location. Spatial mapping is needed because a uniform passivation layer could improve PL without changing the nucleation pathway, whereas a pathway-control mechanism should correlate with local differences in conversion kinetics, grain boundaries, or intermediate-phase distribution. The strongest controls are a chemically inert evaporated layer of similar thickness, a post-anneal surface treatment applied after conversion, and a treatment that does not contain the active ionic organic species. If only the pre-anneal ionic layer changes the intermediate sequence and final microstructure, pathway control is favored. If all treatments that survive annealing give similar PL/QFLS improvements but no kinetic change, passivation or morphology is more likely. Residual uncertainty remains because the evaporated layer may simultaneously modify wetting, ion transport, and defect chemistry; therefore, the conclusion should be tied to the observed kinetic signature rather than inferred solely from final device performance.

Q3

The initial mechanism should be retained but narrowed. The original hypothesis was that X enables a humidity-assisted solid-state conversion through a precursor/perovskite intermediate. The isolated X/PbI2 experiment shows that X can initiate formation of a δ-FAPbI3-like phase at room temperature before the intended high-temperature anneal. That is strong support for the first part of the pathway: X changes the chemical activity of the PbI2-containing precursor and allows a perovskite-related phase to appear under mild conditions. It also supports the idea that the final film is not produced solely by the later thermal step.

However, the result does not prove that ambient humidity is required. In an isolated bilayer, water may be present, absent, or only incidentally available; the observation alone cannot separate a moisture-mediated reaction from a direct X-PbI2 interaction, solvent residue, or another volatile species. It also does not establish whether the room-temperature δ-phase is beneficial, transient, or simply an intermediate that must be converted during subsequent annealing. Therefore humidity should remain a plausible enabling factor, not a confirmed causal variable.

The mechanism should be revised from “humidity-enabled conversion” to “X-initiated low-temperature precursor-to-perovskite conversion, possibly assisted by moisture.” The next controls should compare dry, controlled-humidity, and wet environments; use a chemically similar non-ionic organic layer; vary X thickness; and track the time evolution of PbI2, δ-FAPbI3, and the final α-phase. If the room-temperature phase appears only with X and its kinetics depend on water activity, the humidity-assisted pathway becomes stronger. If it appears under rigorously dry conditions, the mechanism shifts toward direct chemical activation by X. Electronic passivation remains a coupled alternative because improved phase formation can coexist with defect reduction, but it does not explain the appearance of the δ-phase itself.

Q4

The transfer should be judged by whether the same final phase and device-relevant film quality appear under dry conditions, not merely whether X remains on the surface. Three mechanistic classes are plausible. In the first, water is an essential reactant or intermediate-forming species: it hydrates or protonates the precursor, lowers the activation barrier for the solid-state conversion, or participates in a transient hydrated intermediate that collapses into the perovskite during annealing. If this is true, removing water should slow or stop conversion even if X is present. In the second class, water is a kinetic facilitator rather than a stoichiometric reactant: trace moisture changes precursor mobility, local defect chemistry, or nucleation density, allowing X to accelerate conversion but not because water is consumed in a fixed ratio. A small controlled water dose might then reproduce the dry-X result, with diminishing returns above a threshold. In the third class, X primarily passivates defects and improves morphology, while humidity is a correlated processing variable; the dry process could succeed if X still forms the beneficial interfacial chemistry and the anneal supplies enough thermal energy.

Discrimination requires time-resolved and chemically specific measurements at matched temperature and atmosphere. In situ XRD or GIWAXS should track the disappearance of precursor peaks and appearance of perovskite peaks; a humidity-dependent induction time or intermediate peak would support a reaction-pathway role. FTIR/Raman or solid-state NMR could detect hydration, proton transfer, or intermediate species before and after annealing. Isotopic H2O/D2O labeling could reveal whether water-derived atoms enter the product or transient intermediates. Surface-sensitive XPS/UPS/KPFM should test whether X changes work function, ion distribution, or defect signatures independently of conversion. SEM/AFM and cross-sectional microscopy should determine whether morphology changes precede, follow, or coincide with phase formation. A factorial matrix—X/no-X versus dry/humid/N2 with controlled ppm H2O—should include post-anneal water desorption controls so that residual adsorbed water is not mistaken for a reaction participant.

The decisive prediction is therefore conditional. If dry N2 gives complete conversion with the same kinetics and no new intermediates, humidity is not essential under those conditions. If conversion fails or produces a different intermediate unless a minimum water activity is supplied, water is chemically or kinetically required. If a small water dose restores the X-assisted rate but large doses degrade the film, water is a facilitator with a narrow operating window. If X improves PLQY, lifetime, and Voc even when conversion is incomplete, passivation is an independent contribution. The conclusion should remain bounded to the tested precursor composition, layer sequence, annealing schedule, and water-control method.

Q1

The most defensible leading mechanism is that B provides a more effective kinetic barrier against the photoactive-to-nonphotoactive transition through a combination of adsorption geometry, local lattice interaction, and defect passivation, even though C binds more strongly in a simplified surface calculation. The shared fresh-phase and morphology observations rule out gross crystallization failure as the primary reason for B’s advantage. B’s superior delay of the nonphotoactive transformation and resistance to inner-lattice conversion indicate that its molecular orientation or spatial distribution better blocks the structural rearrangement pathway or nucleation sites. Its improved photoluminescence supports concurrent reduction of recombination-active defects, which can also slow degradation by lowering carrier-driven chemical stress. C’s higher calculated adsorption energy and simulated coverage are therefore insufficient descriptors because they do not capture steric accessibility, multidentate coordination, local strain, diffusion barriers, or the actual distribution of molecules at grain boundaries and surfaces.

The strongest competing explanation is that the observed difference arises from an uncontrolled processing variable—such as local concentration, solvent residue, film thickness, precursor complexation, or measurement history—rather than intrinsic molecular structure. A second plausible alternative is that B changes the apparent kinetics without changing the true thermodynamic stability of the photoactive phase; it may simply slow nucleation or ion migration while the final equilibrium remains unfavorable.

Direct structural probes during aging would test whether B raises the nucleation/transition barrier. Thermodynamic measurements or long-time equilibrium studies would be needed to determine whether the free-energy difference itself changes. The supplied observations support kinetic stabilization and passivation, but they do not prove a permanent change in equilibrium phase stability.

Q2

The two isomers should be detected separately in the film by a method that distinguishes their positions, such as isotope-labeled NMR, mass spectrometry after extraction, or spatially resolved spectroscopy, rather than relying on the nominal precursor ratio. If the structural response follows the measured fraction of one isomer, geometry-specific incorporation is supported; if it follows total nitrogen content regardless of isomer identity, generic passivation is more likely.

Temperature-dependent diffraction or scattering can test whether one isomer suppresses octahedral tilting or lowers the activation barrier for the orthorhombic-to-tetragonal transition. Molecular dynamics or quasielastic measurements can determine whether the effect is a change in lattice vibrations, ion mobility, or defect-mediated relaxation. If B stabilizes the framework through geometry-specific coupling, its benefit should appear in both the dynamic response and the delayed formation of degradation products, even when the initial absorption spectrum is similar for B and C. Conversely, if both isomers give nearly identical phase retention despite different populations, the mechanism may be dominated by a shared functional group or by a process unrelated to positional geometry.

Perfect single-variable isolation is unlikely because the salts can alter crystallization, residual strain, surface chemistry and ionic distribution simultaneously. Therefore, the strongest conclusion requires convergent evidence: independent quantification of each isomer, a monotonic structure-dynamics relationship, and phase-stability data that cannot be explained by a single generic descriptor.

Two critical limitations must be stated explicitly. First, the NMR experiment probes a specific deuteration and timescale; it is not a direct measurement of the full phase-transition pathway, activation energy, or long-term device degradation. Second, the molecular-salt identity and concentration are not uniquely isolated from possible changes in crystallization, residual solvent, surface coverage, or ionic impurities. Q4

The absorber result should be interpreted as a partial success. If the B-treated film retains its alpha-phase diffraction pattern and does not show the characteristic delta-FAPbI3 signatures after the same thermal stress, then B has improved the intrinsic phase stability of the perovskite layer under those conditions. The observed loss can therefore arise outside the absorber even when the absorber itself remains phase-pure.

Plausible non-absorber channels include: (1) transport-layer degradation or increased resistance, such as oxidation or thermal decomposition of the hole-transport material, changes in its work function, or formation of an insulating interfacial layer; (2) electrode diffusion or reaction, especially from a reactive metal contact into the perovskite or transport layer; (3) interfacial delamination or void formation caused by different thermal-expansion coefficients or volatile species; (4) light- and bias-driven ion redistribution that changes local stoichiometry, band bending, or recombination even without a bulk phase transition; and (5) encapsulation failure or moisture/oxygen ingress if the test is not hermetically controlled.

Localization requires matched diagnostics on the complete device and on separated layers. In situ or periodic XRD/GIWAXS should confirm whether the absorber remains alpha-phase during MPP. PL/TRPL and electroluminescence can track nonradiative recombination and charge-transfer efficiency. Temperature-dependent impedance, dark J-V, and transient photocurrent/photovoltage can identify rising series resistance, interfacial barriers, or ion-migration signatures. Post-aging cross-sectional SEM/TEM and ToF-SIMS should look for delamination, voids, and elemental interdiffusion. Contact work-function measurements and transport-layer spectroscopy can detect chemical or electronic changes. A control using the same transport stack but without B, and a control with B but a more robust electrode/encapsulation, would help separate absorber from contact contributions.

The apparently reassuring result is the stable absorber phase. It is insufficient because it does not measure device voltage, fill factor, contact resistance, ion redistribution, or encapsulation integrity. Conversely, a device that retains high PCE while the absorber shows phase conversion would point to a compensating contact effect or measurement artifact and would require deeper scrutiny. The defensible conclusion is that B improves one identified instability channel—alpha/delta phase transformation—but the remaining MPP loss must be assigned through stack-resolved evidence rather than assumed to originate in the perovskite lattice.

Q1

The reported correlation between water uptake, conversion kinetics and final electronic quality supports this chain but does not prove it because those variables were not independently controlled.

A second possibility is that M changes nucleation density or annealing kinetics without substantially changing water uptake.

The diagnosis remains provisional because the supplied observations do not separate these routes. Independent tests should vary ambient humidity while holding film thickness constant, vary thickness while holding humidity constant, and measure water uptake, intermediate-phase distribution, conversion rate and electronic quality separately. In situ depth-resolved diffraction or microscopy, spatially resolved thickness/water-content maps, and controls with structurally related non-coordinating additives would be needed. Q2

It would lower water uptake, suppress PbI2 hydration, reduce local humidity gradients and improve the uniformity of the inorganic scaffold. Its effect should therefore be visible in early precursor-film thickness, water-content or PbI2-phase measurements, and it should persist even if the subsequent organic-salt step were performed rapidly under controlled humidity.

A continued-conversion regulator would instead remain active during the organic-salt coating and annealing. It would change the rate at which FA-containing species penetrate the inorganic layer, the local stoichiometry of the intermediate, the sequence from PbI2 to delta/intermediate phases and finally to alpha-FAPbI3, and the spatial distribution of residual PbI2 or non-perovskite phases. Its signature should appear during the second step and should depend on the timing, solvent, concentration and diffusion path of the organic salt.

Time-resolved GIWAXS or XRD during coating and annealing is central because it can follow the disappearance of PbI2, appearance of intermediate phases and growth of alpha-FAPbI3. Depth-resolved GIWAXS, cross-sectional microscopy or ToF-SIMS should map whether conversion proceeds uniformly through the film or leaves buried PbI2-rich regions. In situ optical absorption or PL can track crystallization kinetics, while humidity-controlled experiments can separate moisture suppression from chemical regulation. A matched control without M, a post-coating addition of M, and a chemically similar but non-interacting additive would test whether M must be present in the inorganic precursor and whether its role is specific. If M acts mainly as a barrier, removing it from the inorganic precursor should strongly impair the first step even when the organic step is unchanged. If it continues to regulate conversion, adding it later or changing the organic-salt exposure should alter the phase pathway and final film quality. The strongest conclusion requires both temporal and depth profiles, because a barrier and a conversion regulator can coincidentally improve final morphology.

Q3

Q4

Q1

A bounded leading mechanism is selective halide exchange during vapour-solid conversion. The evaporated PbI2/PbBr2 scaffold first presents a mixed-halide surface. When exposed to an iodide-rich organic-halide vapour, the outermost region converts first into a perovskite-rich layer. Because the incoming vapour is iodide-rich and because the newly formed perovskite surface can act as a reactive sink, bromide in the converting region is displaced or diluted while iodide is incorporated. The conversion front then advances inward, leaving behind a perovskite film whose composition reflects the integrated history of this moving reaction zone rather than the initial scaffold stoichiometry. This explains why the final film remains iodide-rich despite substantial scaffold bromide, why elemental analysis shows strong bromide depletion, and why interrupted samples show a perovskite-rich surface layer over unconverted precursor. The PL/XRD signatures of a perovskite phase and the EDX trend are consistent with progressive formation of a composition-shifted product, but they do not identify the exact chemical species that carry bromide away.

The strongest serious competitor is that the apparent bromide loss is not caused by selective chemical exchange at the reaction front but instead by nonuniform conversion, preferential volatilization of a bromide-containing species, or a measurement/depth-bias artifact. For example, if the iodide-rich vapour reacts faster with certain scaffold regions, the measured average could appear bromide-depleted even without a selective exchange mechanism. Alternatively, a volatile bromide-containing intermediate could escape during processing, or the surface-sensitive measurements could overrepresent an iodide-rich converted skin. These alternatives must be considered because no species-resolved gas-phase measurement or isotopic halide mass balance is available.

Therefore, the causal chain should be stated as follows: vapour-solid conversion creates a moving perovskite-rich front; the local halide environment at that front is dominated by the incoming iodide-rich source; bromide is progressively depleted relative to iodide during front advancement; the final film inherits the integrated composition of this process. The evidence supports this sequence at the level of spatial conversion and bulk composition change. It does not establish which molecular species transport bromide, whether the exchange is purely solid-state, whether a volatile bromide intermediate forms, or whether the measured depletion is partly an analytical depth effect. A decisive test would combine isotopically labelled halides, time-resolved depth profiling, and direct identification of gas-phase products under controlled conversion conditions.

Q2

The decisive test is whether the total amount of each halide in the final film matches the stoichiometric prediction from the initial scaffold and organic-source inventories. If the scaffold contains excess Cl while the organic source supplies Br, a moving reaction front should convert PbCl2-rich regions into mixed-halide perovskite and release the surplus Cl as volatile species. The expected signatures are: (1) a spatially resolved compositional gradient that follows the direction of organic-vapour penetration; (2) a corresponding decrease in the Cl/Pb ratio and increase in Br/Pb ratio with depth; (3) detection of Cl-containing gas or condensate during processing; and (4) a closed mass balance between the measured loss of Cl and the gain of Br in the solid product. Selective conversion alone would produce a composition gradient but not necessarily a net loss of the excess halide from the system. Residual-phase localization would leave Cl-rich PbCl2 or other non-perovskite domains concentrated in specific regions, which could be identified by phase-sensitive mapping rather than averaged composition. Sampling bias would appear if different depths, spots, or beam-damaged areas give inconsistent compositions without a coherent front-to-back trend. Therefore, the experiment should combine depth-resolved XPS/ToF-SIMS or similar chemical profiling with phase mapping, gas analysis, and independent quantification of the starting scaffold and organic source. A strong result would show that the final perovskite composition tracks the predicted halide exchange and that the missing halide is accounted for outside the film. What would remain unresolved is the microscopic transport mechanism—whether Cl leaves as atomic species, molecular complexes, or through coupled diffusion—and the extent to which local strain, defects, or transient intermediates control the front velocity. It would also not establish whether the same mechanism operates under all temperatures, pressures, or organic-source chemistries.

Q4

The first diagnostic task is to separate the buried contact from the absorber before assigning device loss. Contact retention can be probed by washing or dissolving the perovskite after controlled ageing and quantifying the remaining phosphonic-acid species on ITO by XPS, ToF-SIMS depth profiling, or mass spectrometry. The identity of degradation products should also be measured because cleavage of the organic scaffold can leave fragments that still anchor or block transport. Absorber damage should be assessed independently by PLQY, TRPL, XRD/GIWAXS, SEM/AFM, and chemical analysis for PbI2, iodine-related species, or scaffold-derived residues. Conversely, if the contact remains intact while PLQY and morphology deteriorate, absorber photochemistry dominates. Trade-offs include thicker UV filters reducing current, stronger anchors increasing resistance or roughness, and passivants altering energy alignment. The diagnosis remains incomplete if ageing is performed only in one atmosphere, illumination spectrum, temperature, or device architecture, because bond cleavage and perovskite photochemistry can be environment-dependent.

Q1

The combined effect should lower local leakage and slow the onset of irreversible reverse-bias damage. Q2

The decisive variable is whether the molecular layer remains continuous under the local topography of ITO. Route S can leave valleys uncovered because a solution film cannot conform perfectly to every protrusion and recess. Route E can drive molecules into those recesses through field-assisted adsorption, while Route EF can additionally modify the local chemistry. If continuity is the dominant cause, the improvement should appear first as reduced local leakage and fewer pinhole-like failure sites, followed by more uniform nucleation of the perovskite and lower shunt density.

Atomic-force microscopy or conductive AFM should map the molecular coverage directly on rough ITO, with particular attention to valley bottoms and grain boundaries. Kelvin-probe force microscopy can test whether work-function modification is uniform rather than patchy. Contact-angle measurements on the coated ITO should determine whether the molecular layer changes wetting enough to alter perovskite precursor spreading. Cross-sectional SEM or ToF-SIMS should then verify that the perovskite covers the substrate without voids and that the molecular species remains at the intended interface after deposition.

Electrical diagnostics should be performed on matched devices. Dark current-voltage curves, ideality factors, light-intensity-dependent Voc, impedance spectra and local electroluminescence or photoluminescence mapping can distinguish shunt-dominated loss from bulk recombination. The reverse-bias test is especially important: if Route E/EF suppresses leakage and maintains voltage under reverse stress while Route S fails locally, the continuity hypothesis is strengthened. A control using a different molecular contact with similar dipole but poorer adhesion would help separate generic passivation from the specific electrodeposition advantage.

A non-diagnostic observation would be a higher average PCE alone. That result could arise from better wetting, altered perovskite crystallization, improved energy alignment, reduced trap density or simply a thicker absorber. Without direct maps showing that Route E fills the same valleys left bare by Route S, and without correlated local leakage suppression, the performance gain cannot be assigned to continuous coverage. Similarly, a change in surface potential without corresponding improvement in reverse-bias leakage would indicate energetic tuning rather than the proposed robustness mechanism. The strongest conclusion requires concordance among topography-resolved coverage, uniform interfacial energetics, controlled perovskite morphology and device-level suppression of shunts and reverse-bias degradation.

Route E should show fewer dark-current hot spots, more uniform electroluminescence, and lower local shunt density across the full module area than Route S, even where the nominal molecular coverage is similar. Reverse-bias breakdown should shift from discrete low-voltage punctures to a higher, more uniform threshold, and the distribution of local breakdown voltages should narrow. Module yield should improve because isolated pinholes and edge defects are eliminated rather than because every grain boundary is chemically passivated.

A passivation-dominated explanation would predict that the largest gains occur at chemically active sites and that devices with comparable coverage but different functional groups differ strongly in Voc, ideality factor, trap density, and recombination lifetime. If Route EF outperforms Route E mainly through additional chemical interaction, then a nonfunctionalized but continuous Route-E-like layer should retain some continuity benefit but lose the extra voltage/recombination gain. A film-quality explanation would require the overlying perovskite to change systematically: larger grains, fewer voids, altered orientation, or reduced buried-interface strain. In that case, identical molecular contacts deposited on deliberately varied perovskite films should reproduce the performance trend.

The continuity-only model is falsified if Route E has the same coverage and no hot-spot reduction yet still improves Voc and fill factor, or if a continuous Route-S analogue performs as well as Route E. It is also weakened if the gain disappears when the functional group is removed despite unchanged morphology, or if the overlying film becomes worse while device metrics improve. The strongest diagnosis therefore combines spatially resolved dark current/electroluminescence, coverage mapping, contact-resistance imaging, chemical-group controls, and cross-sectional film analysis.

A directional gradient and changing Cl/Pb and Br/Pb ratios are necessary but not sufficient. They must be accompanied by a monotonic conversion-front progression and a closed halide balance. Sampling bias would appear if different depths, spots, or beam-damaged areas give inconsistent compositions without a coherent front-to-back trend. Therefore, the experiment should combine depth-resolved XPS/ToF-SIMS or similar chemical profiling with phase mapping, gas analysis, and independent quantification of the starting scaffold and organic source. What would remain unresolved is the microscopic transport mechanism—whether Cl leaves as atomic species, molecular complexes, or through coupled diffusion—and the extent to which local strain, defects, or transient intermediates control the front velocity.
